lab_title: Exploring VSEPR Geometry: Predicting Molecular Shapes from Electron Domains
top_level_objectives: Count electron domains around a central atom from Lewis structures and identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral).
Predict molecular geometries for AXmEn formulas by accounting for bonding vs lone pairs and their distribution among the electron-domain framework.
Explain how lone-pair repulsion alters bond angles and leads to deviations from idealized geometries.
Relate predicted shapes to real molecules (CO2, BF3, CH4, NH3, PF5, SF6, XeF4, H2O) and interpret differences between the predicted and observed structures.
Develop spatial reasoning by manipulating a 3D AR model to arrange electron domains into minimum-repulsion configurations and compare predictions to known molecular geometries.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1 — Foundation: From Lewis structures to electron-domain geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the VSEPR idea and establish how to count electron domains around a central atom. Present the five fundamental electron-domain geometries as the scaffold for predicting shapes.
key_visuals: Central atom with electron-domain markers (bonding pairs as blue spheres, lone pairs as red lobes)
Translucent wireframe representations of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries surrounding the center
Text labels like AX2, AX3, AX4, AX5, AX6 with domain counts
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene1_Intro
student_actions: Identify the central atom on a provided Lewis structure
Count bonding pairs and lone pairs to determine the electron-domain count
Match the count to the corresponding geometry and observe a quick AR visualization of that geometry

scenes.brief_purpose: Show the 180° arrangement that results when there are two electron domains (no lone pairs) around the central atom.
key_visuals: CO2 model with two opposing bonds and a 180° angle labeled
Text labels: AX2 (linear) and 180°
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene2_Linear
student_actions: Place the two bonding domains around the center opposite each other and confirm a linear geometry
Observe and record the bond angle (~180°) and discuss why no lone pairs are present in this case

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3 — Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry (3 domains)
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the 120° arrangement when three electron domains surround the central atom (no lone pairs).
key_visuals: BF3 with three bonds arranged in a planar triangle (~120°)
Text labels: AX3 (trigonal planar) and 120°
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene3_Tr planar
student_actions: Arrange three bonding domains around the center to realize a trigonal planar arrangement
Observe the planar geometry and note the 120° angles; consider how adding lone pairs would modify the shape in a later scene

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 — Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and lone-pair effects
scenes.brief_purpose: Show the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry (4 domains) and illustrate how lone pairs modify molecular geometry within this framework (e.g., NH3).
key_visuals: CH4 displaying a classic tetrahedral arrangement with ~109.5° angles
NH3 showing a trigonal pyramidal shape (AX3E) with one lone pair and adjusted angles
Text labels: AX4 (tetrahedral) and AX3E (trigonal pyramidal)
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene4_Tetrahedral
student_actions: Construct the four bonding domains around the center to realize a tetrahedral geometry (CH4)
Replace one bonding domain with a lone pair to form a trigonal pyramidal geometry (NH3) and observe the reduced angles

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5 — Trigonal bipyramidal geometry and derived shapes
scenes.brief_purpose: Activate the five-electron-domain geometry and demonstrate how lone pairs distribute to produce seesaw and T-shaped geometries.
key_visuals: PF5 in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement highlighting axial and equatorial positions
SF4 showing a seesaw geometry (AX4E) with one lone pair
ClF3 showing a T-shaped geometry (AX3E2) with two lone pairs
Text labels: AX5 (trigonal bipyramidal), AX4E (seesaw), AX3E2 (T-shaped)
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene5_Bipyramidal
student_actions: Create PF5 to observe the trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry
Introduce a single lone pair to obtain a seesaw geometry and note the angular alterations
Add a second lone pair to produce a T-shaped geometry and compare the angles

scenes.brief_purpose: Exhibit the six-electron-domain octahedral geometry and show how lone pairs lead to square pyramidal and square planar shapes.
key_visuals: SF6 with an octahedral arrangement of six ligands
XeF4 illustrating square planar geometry (AX4E2) with two opposite lone pairs
Text labels: AX6 (octahedral), AX4E2 (square planar)
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene6_Octahedral
student_actions: Assemble SF6 to confirm the octahedral geometry
Introduce two lone pairs to yield XeF4’s square planar geometry and compare angles to the ideal

scenes.scene_name: Scene 7 — Real molecules, deviations, and synthesis
scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge predictions with real molecular geometries, discuss how lone-pair repulsion alters angles, and summarize the applicability to common molecules.
key_visuals: Overlay comparing predicted shapes to CO2, BF3, CH4, NH3, PF5, SF6, XeF4 and H2O
Labels noting approximate angles: 180°, 120°, ~109.5°, ~90°, and water’s ~104.5°
Audio clip: VSEPR_Scene7_RealMolecules
student_actions: Compare predicted vs actual molecular geometries; explain angle deviations due to lone-pair repulsion
Summarize key lessons and reflect on the applicability of VSEPR to the listed molecules
